## Evidence check (repo scope)

I inspected `.github/workflows/supercomputer-cluster.yml`, `scripts/cluster_worker.py`, `scripts/aggregate_cluster.py`, and searched for `bubble`/`Rayleigh`/`Keller-Miksis`/`Bjerknes` across the repo. **There is no bubble-dynamics ODE codebase here.** The repo's actual "cluster" is a 12-way matrix of `montecarlo`/`primes`/`hashstorm`/discovery/genealogy shard workers, each writing one JSON artifact, aggregated only **after the whole matrix completes** (a hard completion barrier), with results published via a racy git commit/push retry loop (the aggregator's 5-attempt fetch/reset/push loop). I also found an earlier "lite" review of this same task already sitting in `bridge/outbox/`, which independently reached the same conclusion: no bubble code exists, treat this as pre-implementation design review. My review below is grounded in that real substrate (matrix jobs, artifact upload/download, transactional git publish, issue-triggered dispatch) plus standard numerical-coupling and distributed-systems reasoning — not in any code that exists yet.

**Bottom line up front:** the proposed 12-node "one physics module per node" decomposition is not defensible as described. The current substrate is architecturally a batch/MapReduce pattern (independent shards → barrier → merge); the proposal needs a fine-grained, low-jitter, repeatedly-re-synchronized time-stepping loop. Those are incompatible without either (a) restricting distribution to genuinely loosely-coupled physics, or (b) leaving GitHub-hosted ephemeral runners for the core loop.

---

### (1) Couplings that MUST be same-process, same-step
Radial dynamics (R, Ṙ, R̈) ↔ gas pressure closure ↔ internal heat transfer ↔ interfacial mass/vapor transfer ↔ the shape-mode parametric-driving term. These share one fast, collapse-scale timescale (μs, shrinking further at minimum radius) and are algebraically coupled *at the same instant* inside the ODE/DAE right-hand side (the RP/KM equation needs p_gas(t) and Ṙ(t) simultaneously to evaluate R̈; shape modes are parametrically driven by R(t) at the integrator's own adaptive resolution, not a macrostep-sampled value). This is not a "distribute with a good protocol" problem — any inserted latency here aliases the fast driving term. This block must be one process, one adaptive stepper, one RHS function.

### (2) Couplings safe for multirate/co-simulation
Bubble-bubble acoustics/Bjerknes forces (longer-range, has a *physical* retardation you can model explicitly, not confuse with network delay — see Q4), translation under drag/Bjerknes force, wall/boundary geometric effects, external turbulence/flow field (quasi-steady relative to collapse). These have genuine timescale separation from the core, which is the standard justification (established) for multirate/co-simulation splitting. Interfacial/surfactant physics is ambiguous: safe if it only modulates surface tension slowly; unsafe if it drives fast Marangoni-shape coupling — this needs an explicit justification per use case, not an assumed default.

### (3) Best coupling method
Given (1)/(2), only the slow subsystems are candidates for partitioning. Pure Jacobi (stale, simultaneous exchange) is the weakest choice and specifically dangerous here because "staleness" on GH Actions is dominated by artifact/API latency (seconds, highly variable), not a small deliberate window. Gauss-Seidel reduces this but imposes an arbitrary evaluation order (bias unless alternated). **Recommended: predictor-corrector at each macrostep, with a bounded number of correction iterations (a truncated waveform relaxation)** — predict the coupling variable via extrapolation to hide communication latency, integrate, then correct once real data arrives, checking a fixed-point residual. Full waveform relaxation to convergence is the more rigorous, literature-established technique (Lelarasmee et al.-style, later applied to FMI/multiphysics co-simulation) but requires cheap re-integration/rollback per iteration — expensive when "re-iterate" means booting another ephemeral VM. Cap iterations (e.g., 3) and fall back to macrostep halving instead of iterating indefinitely.

### (4) Preventing communication delay from becoming fake physics
The critical rule: **exchanged data must be tagged and ordered by simulated time/macrostep index, never by wall-clock arrival order.** Concretely: (a) coordinator advances simulated time only when all required macrostep-n data is present, independent of how long that took in real seconds; (b) never substitute "most recently arrived" for "most recently valid" — this is a classic logical-vs-physical-clock ordering bug (Lamport); (c) on missed deadlines, extrapolate via the node's own predictor rather than silently waiting — an implicit wait lets GH Actions' variable queueing/artifact-round-trip delay act as a stochastic transport-delay term, which produces spurious oscillations that mimic delay-differential-equation instability, not real physics; (d) detect this empirically via conservation drift correlated with wall-clock jitter rather than macrostep count (see Q9's latency-injection test — this is the single most important falsification check for the stated design goal).

### (5) Transport mechanism
Artifacts (upload-after-job-completes, download-in-dependent-job) match the current workflow's batch/barrier pattern and are structurally wrong for "periodic exchange during the run" — the aggregator only reads artifacts once the whole matrix finishes. Issue-based queues add webhook/API latency (seconds–minutes) and hit rate limits under repeated exchange. Repo-as-broker (git commit/push) already shows its own race in the existing 5-attempt retry loop; doing that every macrostep for every loosely-coupled node does not scale. An external lightweight broker (queue/object store/HTTP endpoint) removes the git-serialization bottleneck but doesn't fix the underlying problem: **GH-hosted runners have no queueing-time SLA and are ephemeral**, so you'd need one long-lived polling job per node rather than one job per macrostep, bounded by the 6-hour job cap. **Recommendation: self-hosted runner(s) or a single persistent local/VM coordinator process for the tightly coupled core and any sub-second exchange; GH-hosted matrix jobs remain legitimate only for the slow/loosely-coupled peripheral modules** (per-bubble ensemble members, external field precompute, parameter sweeps) — i.e., reuse GH Actions for what it's actually good at (the repo's existing embarrassingly-parallel pattern), not for the fine-grained loop.

### (6) Synchronization protocol / convergence / rollback / checkpoint / conservation
- **Protocol:** Bulk-Synchronous-Parallel macrostep barrier — nodes integrate locally to t_n+Δt using predicted boundary data, report; coordinator computes coupling residual; accept or trigger a bounded predictor-corrector re-iteration; only then advance n.
- **Convergence criterion:** relative change in exchanged coupling variables between iterations < ε, *and* conservation residual (below) within tolerance; cap iterations, fall back to halving Δt_macro if not met — an extrapolation of adaptive-stepsize control (established for single-integrator error control) applied at the coupling level (this generalization is engineering judgment, not a textbook-cited technique — flag accordingly).
- **Rollback:** each node's microstep integration must be a pure function of (state at t_n, this macrostep's boundary data) so it can be re-run deterministically from a saved checkpoint; only the coordinator holds the authoritative committed-state history.
- **Checkpoint format:** extend the existing `worker-*.json` / `cluster/latest.json` pattern with `macrostep`, `sim_time`, per-module state vector (units/frame documented), coupling-variable provenance (which iteration produced it), and a content hash — this repo already has the right shape for this, it just lacks time-stepping fields.
- **Conservation checks:** total energy budget (kinetic + gas internal + radiated − dissipated), dissolved-gas/vapor mass balance, momentum for translating/interacting bubbles — checked every macrostep. Monitoring interface energy exchange as the coupling-artifact diagnostic is standard partitioned-coupling practice (Farhat/Piperno-style FSI literature: explicit interface coupling is a known source of spurious energy injection/damping).

### (7) Node mapping
The "one physics term per node" mapping is the wrong decomposition axis given (1). Recommended: **1 node/process = the entire tightly coupled core (radial + gas thermo + heat + mass transfer + shape-mode driving term), monolithic.** Remaining nodes: one per interacting bubble in a many-bubble ensemble (Bjerknes/acoustics — this actually fits GH Actions' existing embarrassingly-parallel-with-light-coupling strength), one for external turbulence/flow precompute, one for wall/boundary geometry, one coordinator for conservation/convergence/rollback (mirrors the existing prepare/aggregate roles), remainder used for parameter/ensemble sweeps rather than physics-term splitting. **Decompose over bubbles/parameters, not over terms of one bubble's stiff ODE.**

### (8) What the prototype should implement first
Exactly the reference already sketched in this repo's prior lite review: a single-process, single-bubble monolithic integrator (RP baseline + Keller-Miksis at low Mach, same interface), validated against closed-form Minnaert frequency and Rayleigh collapse time, adaptive RK45/DOP853, tolerance-convergence sweep. Only after this monolithic ground truth is validated should one genuinely loosely-coupled module (a second Bjerknes-coupled bubble, or a slow external field) be added as the first distributed co-simulation test case — otherwise the "distributed vs monolithic" comparison in (9) has nothing to falsify against.

### (9) Falsifiable validation plan
1. Monolithic reference (tight tolerance) vs distributed version, identical parameters/ICs/Δt_macro; trajectory error (R(t), Ṙ(t), p_gas, T) under a pre-committed norm and tolerance (e.g., <1% peak collapse error) — exceedance or *unbounded growth over cycles* falsifies the claim.
2. **Latency-injection test:** vary wall-clock exchange delay while holding simulated Δt_macro fixed; trajectory must be invariant to wall-clock latency alone. If it isn't, (4) is falsified — this is the test that directly targets the stated design goal.
3. Conservation-drift comparison: distributed residual growth rate must not exceed monolithic's pure-integration drift.
4. Ablation: predictor-corrector disabled (pure stale Jacobi) vs enabled — must show measurably worse error, confirming the corrector isn't a no-op.
5. Restrict the primary pass/fail regime to non-chaotic forcing amplitudes; treat strongly nonlinear/near-chaotic collapse as a separate, wider-tolerance stress test (RP/KM sensitivity there can masquerade as coupling error).

### (10) Hidden assumption most likely to cause failure
The proposal implicitly assumes communication latency and required physical coupling bandwidth are independently tunable — that a good enough protocol (predictor-corrector, convergence checks) can always compensate for whatever round-trip delay the substrate imposes. That's false specifically near inertial collapse: the core subsystem timescales compress by orders of magnitude in microseconds, so the *required* exchange resolution shrinks exactly when GH Actions' *achievable* exchange latency (job scheduling, artifact round trips, API rate limits — realistically seconds) is fixed and cannot shrink. This is a hard bandwidth mismatch, not an implementation detail solvable by a smarter protocol — which is why the core must be monolithic regardless of synchronization sophistication.

---

**Summary recommendation:** keep GH Actions for what the repo already does well (12-way embarrassingly-parallel ensemble/parameter sweeps, barrier-aggregated); do not distribute the fast bubble-interior ODE/DAE core across ephemeral runners at all; use a self-hosted or single persistent coordinator process for that core; reserve genuine node-to-node coupling for slow, physically separated subsystems (multi-bubble acoustics, external flow, boundary effects) using predictor-corrector/bounded waveform relaxation with simulated-time-tagged messages and mandatory latency-injection + conservation-drift tests before trusting any result as "coupled dynamics" rather than latency-induced artifact.
